summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity. No instrument reviewed for this record creates such an offence at regional level either. The visitor-facing risk in the region is structural rather than statutory: it arises from which forum hears a dispute and which body of personal law applies, not from any provision aimed at gender non-conformity.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, begun 29 March 2019 and published by the Bangsamoro Official Gazette, prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause reads: 'in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws'. A trans visitor's dispute can therefore be routed into a forum applying Shari'ah or traditional law rather than the civil framework that governs elsewhere in the Philippines.

On 14 July 2026 the Bangsamoro Parliament proposed a Shari'ah Justice Code of 10 books that would extend Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status law confined since PD 1083 (1977) into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution, resting on BOL authority and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums with written-opt-in clauses for civil entities. A visitor married to a Muslim spouse enters this legal-pluralist marriage regime, in which the recognition of that marriage and of the visitor's status is decided under Shari'ah personal law rather than the civil rules applied elsewhere in the country.

In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; the Bangsamoro Parliament passed it unanimously. The measure carries Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing, so the forum question a trans visitor faces in this region is not confined to it.
tangentialFactors:
The expansion of Shari'ah courts in August 2024 was reported with local Christian-leader reaction, indicating that the reach of religious personal law is contested in the surrounding provinces as well as inside the autonomous region.

The proposed Shari'ah Justice Code of 14 July 2026 would move Shari'ah jurisdiction from personal status into civil and commercial matters, widening the range of disputes in which a visitor's case could be heard in a Shari'ah forum rather than a civil one.
localsOnly:
For Muslim residents of the Bangsamoro, marriage, divorce, succession and family relations are governed by Shari'ah forums, with written-opt-in clauses allowing civil entities to opt into the civil regime; this legal-pluralist arrangement is a resident-facing feature of the region's personal-law order.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13 guarantees religious freedom and structures regional governance with a justice-dispensation clause reading 'in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws', which governs how regional institutions dispense justice for residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
No region-specific incident of violence, discrimination enforcement, or facilities practice targeting trans people in the Bangsamoro was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment carried by the parent record applies in that respect.

The proposed Shari'ah Justice Code was still a proposal as of 14 July 2026; whether it has been enacted, and in what final form, is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

The sources do not state how Shari'ah personal-law forums in the Bangsamoro would treat a trans person's gender marker, marital status, or a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status; that question is not sourced here.
